utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On this Wednesday, the 7th of February, 2007, I'd like to greet all those present from the courtroom. The Prosecution, that is complete. The Defence counsel, the accused, and the witness. We're going to continue the testimony, but before I do so I'd like to give the floor to the registrar for IC numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Two parties have submitted lists of documents through Witness DC. The list submitted by OTP shall be given Exhibit number IC 372 under seal, while the list submitted by 3D shall be given Exhibit number IC 373. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Yes, the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Good afternoon to Your Honours and to everybody else in the court. Before we broke yesterday afternoon it occurred to me that I had omitted to ask for IC numbers for two screen shots that the witness was presented with and gave certain evidence. The first one -- both of the screen shots were extracts from Exhibit 09139, and the first one, if you may remember, was the screen shot which displayed the telegraph pole. That wasn't marked. And the second one was the angle shot of the alleyway in which the witness put an X on where he thought the police post was located. I kindly ask Your Honours for an IC number for both of those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. The first picture will become IC 374, while the second one, second photograph, will become IC 375.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We're going to start off with -- well, we were going to start off request a question from the bench but there is no point in asking it now because the witness already answered it in response to Mr. Praljak's question. I am going to give the floor, without further ado to the Defence to start off the cross-examination. I don't know what order they're going to take it in. Who is going to start? Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I would like to follow on from a point that arose at the end of last night. You said in the course of your evidence yesterday, when you were asked about the entry/exit wounds, you said, "I can't see to the back of my leg to see the exit wound. You can see the entry wound very clearly." Now, I want to give you the opportunity to think and make sure we have this absolutely straight. Are you saying that the exit wound is in the back of your leg?

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understood you to say that I said that the exit wound was at the back of my knee, whereas it was the other way around. The entry wound was at the back, and the exit wound was in front. So you can see the traces of the exit wound of the bullet. Now, where -- at the back where the entry wound is, I didn't see that, nor can I see that now. Nor could any of you see what there is on the opposite side of your knee, or the back side of your knee. So let me repeat. The entry wound was at the back.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Witness, that's clear. It isn't what you said yesterday, but I'm not quibbling about that, I just wanted to get it plain today and give you that opportunity. Now, when you were at home before you went to the bridge that evening, you said in your statement that you were meant to start your shift sometime that evening. And you mean your -- your military shift, don't you?

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I mean. My military shift. And I forgot to say yesterday that I went to fetch my daughter's medicines during the day for the precise reason that in the evening I was supposed to take up my shift duty. I can't remember the exact time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, that --

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Have I been clear?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, yes. My next question is to ask if -- even though you can't say the exact time, can you remember the approximate time when you were due to start your shift?

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't remember. I -- it was to be a night shift, but as to the exact time, I really don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Where -- where were you actually to work on your shift? Was it -- first of all, was it at one fixed location that your shift work was to take place?

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mostly I stood guard in the area of Donja Mahala, around my house. However, there were a number of guard posts, so we would change around. And that was the practice, that you stood guard at different locations from time to time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So is this right: You did -- you wouldn't have known until you reported for duty that evening exactly where you would be sent? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I knew. Sometimes you knew it in advance, but on that particular night I don't think I did know in advance.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Where did you actually have to report to at the beginning of your shift?

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat, I really don't know what time I started doing my shift duty. It was to have been a night shift, but when I took over the shift, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I think there was some misunderstanding about my question. My question was, where did you have to report to?

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, to the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And was that the same side of the river as your house or on the other side?

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The eastern side of the river, and of my house, if you mean the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I mean where it was you had to report to. That's clear, isn't it? So where you had to report to was on the east side of the river, correct?

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The right bank. The right bank of the river, that's West Mostar. The right bank of the Neretva River, that's where the command was, on the right bank, and that is considered -- there must have been a slip there, that's considered to be West Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's fine, witness. We cleared that. So it follows then, does it, that where you had to report for duty was on the same side of the river as where you lived?

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: How old was your daughter at the time?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stewart, we're trying to understand and to follow. What is the importance of the precise hour at which he stood guard and the age of his daughter with respect to where he was when he was hit by the bullet. As we've already said, there are just two things that we are interested in here, precisely: The direction of the shot and the location of the victim. Everything else is secondary.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, there is one point that may be considered secondary but important to the examiner is to test the veracity and credibility of the witness. That is a fair approach, Your Honour, and may I proceed doing that? My questions are not irrelevant or I wouldn't ask them, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Witness, your daughter was 19 years old, she had been wounded, I think you said three days previously. Had she had hospital treatment when she was wounded?

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally put her in to a car and risking our lives, both of our lives, I drove her to the local commune, which is on the same bank, the same side, I don't know if you know Mostar, but it's about 300 metres away from my house by car taking the main road and from Stotina you can see the road and the sniper or snipers, I don't know, didn't expect anybody to be that much of a fool, to move around that road in broad daylight. So we were lucky to get there. Anyway, I went to the local commune, and they gave her first aid, which is to say they just bandaged up the wound with an ordinary bandage, and then I took her back home straight away. And with the first group of wounded through UNPROFOR she was transported to Turkey. However, not even there did she receive adequate medical aid and assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, Witness, you told the Trial Chamber yesterday that your neighbour, whom I won't name, but your neighbour who accompanied you across the bridge was wearing civilian clothing, and you indicated that the reason why he was wearing civilian clothing was to reduce the risk of his being sniped at when he crossed the bridge. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that I told you the reason for which he was wearing any kind of clothing or civilian clothing. I spoke about myself. I said that I wanted to be dressed as lightly as possible, to be able to run across the bridge better. Why he was wearing civilian clothes, well I don't think I said that. I didn't consult him on that issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Is it -- excuse me, Your Honour. You said, "I don't think he was wearing military uniform, precisely because he was afraid of snipers while crossing the bridge." Now, those are your precise words. So do you agree that seems to bear out the suggestion I have made that that was a reason that you gave for his wearing civilian clothes - that implies clearly, doesn't it? - to reduce the danger to him from crossing the bridge? Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's logical. Logical.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So what's also logical then, do you agree, is that it clearly was his view that there was a lower risk for civilians crossing the bridge than there was for people who were identifiably military?

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether I said that there were very little military uniforms and very few soldiers, very few of them had any army uniforms. Whether he had an army uniform at all, I don't know, I don't think he did. And I don't think he was wearing a military uniform in crossing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: There comes a point when I can leave logic to the judges and we can stick to the facts with to you. You described, if I recall it - it is correct, is it? - that when you crossed the bridge, you did actually run, did you, from pillar to pillar, stopping at each of those large pillars? Is that the way that you crossed the bridge?

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember saying I stood by every pillar, but just that I used the pillars as shelter and to try and confuse the sniper. So we would stay 10, 15 seconds, 20 seconds by some of the pillars, thinking that we would trick the sniper in that way so that they wouldn't know when we would emerge from what pillar.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And your neighbour adopted the same technique, did he for crossing the bridge? He stopped, at least, behind some of the pillars and waited before dashing forward? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure, but I think he applied the same tactics. I wasn't following him, I was doing my best to take shelter and hide and it was only once I had left the bridge and was on the left bank that I could see him and see what he was doing. But that's what we had agreed beforehand, that that's the tactics we would apply in order to protect ourselves from the sniper fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thinking back, can you remember any reason at all why your neighbour should have gone with you on this particular excursion to fetch medicine for your daughter?

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know the reason why he went to town, but I use -- seized the opportunity. Now, who suggested that we should go first, I don't know. I know why I went. Now why he went into town, I really can't say. He went on a -- he had some private business to see what was going on, on the left bank because we were isolated, two or 300 metres from where we were, we didn't know what was happening. So we didn't know what was happening on the other bank. And I thought he was just curious to see what was going on, on the other side. Now, whether he had any relatives there or not and that was an additional reason, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment. Mr. Stewart, looking at the time, I assume that you have been allotted extra time by your colleagues, have you?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I haven't. But, Your Honour, my position is this: I don't have very many more questions but the questions which I do have, and my next one will certainly indicate that, go absolutely critically to the heart of what it is that this Trial Chamber needs to know from this witness. May I put the next question, Your Honour, and Your Honour will see where we are going and how important it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Witness, what you have described about your going to the bridge and the way in which you crossed the bridge, dashing from pillar to pillar, do you agree that that shows very clearly that you regarded crossing this bridge at that time as extremely dangerous?

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell you that you are very lucky not to have been in my skin then. You would have risked your life and I risked my life and even more so perhaps the life of my daughter, so I went consciously, I took the risk consciously and you ought to know, and I assume that you weren't ever in such a situation, but life was cheap. So I didn't think about myself and my life too much, but to save my daughter's arm.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Witness, you agreed that it was dangerous to cross the bridge. What was the danger you were afraid of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know how many times I have to repeat this. A sniper, whether it was an ordinary rifle or sniper, I can't go that far and say which it was, but that's what I was afraid of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I want to get it clear, Witness. It's just your own description of your own activities that indicate how dangerous you considered it to be, dashing from pillar to pillar, but it was so -- the need for your daughter who had not been hospitalised apparently, had got first aid, the need for your daughter to have medicines on that particular afternoon, was so compelling that you were prepared to risk leaving her fatherless by crossing this dangerous bridge. Is that what we are to understand?

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, I entreat you, could you mention my daughter as little as possible, please. I said, and I will say it again today, I was ready to give my life. What would happen afterwards, I didn't give it that much thought. She had a mother. Now, what would happen to me, that wasn't what I was thinking at that time. I didn't give that much thought.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stewart --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I finish what I was saying?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stewart, could you stay what you wish to show us, because it seems we've lost 20 minutes of our time, up to now. With all due respect, we haven't advanced not even by a millimetre. I'm sure you have a goal in mind, so show it. Because this is 20 minutes wasted. I'm sure you're going ask a question that will throw light on this matter because so far we are in the fog.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I will proceed and try to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And let me add, all the more so, since from the very beginning the witness explained that there were these pillars on the bridge and that he used the pillars to protect himself. So for us it was quite obvious that the passage across the bridge was dangerous. That was in evidence from the very beginning, and yet you're coming back to that question. And there was not a shadow of doubt that to cross the bridge you ran a great danger. It wasn't for his own pleasure that he crossed the bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour seems, with respect, to be expressing conclusions which normally would wait until the end of the evidence. But Your Honour I'm not going to enter into argument in the presence of the witness about the -- about where all this matter leads. In due course, all the threads of everybody's cases will be tied together.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Witness, you said in your statement that people were blowing up bridges at that time, and you have indicated that this bridge was being guarded. So there was more military activity in relation to this bridge than sniping, wasn't there, according to you?

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honours. With respect, my recollection was that the witness gave evidence that there were policemen on both sides of the bridge, policemen ununiformed on the Donja Mahala side, and policemen with uniforms on the Luka side. There was no mention that there were any military whatsoever anywhere near this bridge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Petkovic. Just a moment, Mr. Stewart. Your client is on his feet. Mr. Petkovic, perhaps you're going throw some light on all this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to point to a fact. We cannot speak about a policeman as if some -- as being something alien to an armed struggle. A policeman who belonged to the BH Army to the Muslim people, to the MUP, is a member of the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina by the same token. So to say that he was unarmed, that's just a story. That's the first point. When my counsel asked the question, I gained the impression that here in this courtroom what is said is this: What wasn't on the Bulevar, that the civilians were in-depth. Now you have the front-line and you have the depth. What is in-depth? A battalion might have its line, and then one kilometre in-depth. We heard that there was the Medical Corps over there and various other -- the ZIS was over there too. So the main infantry firing goes to a depth of at least 400 metres. And that that's where there are civilians, whereas it seems that we're looking at the matter like this: If you have left the front-line, all the rest is civilians. Now this is somebody who is running across a military bridge so nobody can know if he is running across the bridge to fetch ammunition. I don't want you to take this as criticism, but it seems to me that everybody here thinks that unless people are at the front-line, all the rest were civilians. Whereas the firing was firing within a range of 400 metres and it can be successful even further than that. That's what a military science tells us. So the targets are not only up at the front-line where you have one soldier next to another soldier but it is in this whole range and surrounding area where you don't only have only civilians. So I'm glad that we are going to have an expert witness who's going to address these matters. That's what I wanted to point out, because I felt the need to do so. So we cannot say that the apart from the front-line, all the rest, all the rest of the area is filled with civilians. The BH army, the brigade of the BH Army took up its positions in the whole of East Mostar, and deployed its men all around, its armed forces. So I would really like a military expert to come into court to say how this brigade deployed. A mortar shooting from two kilometres is in town, he is part of the combat, and then by the same token, he can be targeted as well. That's what I wanted to explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: My client --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're going to have the floor in just a moment, Mr. Stewart. But I'd like -- would just like to say that that did not escape me, and from the beginning of the cross-examination, and the testimony, I asked the witness to which unit of the BH Army he belonged to, and he explained, he said that he belonged to -- I'm talking from memory now, I think he said he belonged to the 2nd Battalion, was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, 1st Company, 2nd Battalion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There we have it. So your preoccupations, Mr. Petkovic, are those which the judges are already thinking about and have in their heads. And I even asked the witness where the 2nd Battalion was and he told me that he was providing security for the area of Donja Mahala. So your preoccupations are something that we have already thought about. You expressed them in military terms but it did not escape us that when you have the front-line, you have an occupation in-depth into the BH and ABiH. Having said that, Mr. Stewart, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm very much obliged, Your Honour. I would just like to say I am completely at one with my client, which is a happy situation to be in, on what he said. And that was all in response to an objection by Mr. Flynn to a question which, in fact, I see was -- was precisely and carefully put by me. I didn't suggest it was anybody other than policemen guarding the bridge, but I did put it to the witness that there was more military activity in relation to this bridge than sniping. And, Your Honour, where the witness has himself said that there were people blowing up bridges, it would be an extremely narrow interpretation of the word "military" for that not to be properly embraced in my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So my question is, Witness, that there was -- there was more violent activity in relation to this bridge, wasn't there, than just sniping?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Stewart, where is the foundation? Who has ever alleged any violent action? It was said that bridges were blown up, and that precautions were being taken against this particular bridge being blown up. But I cannot regard this as a violent action. Where is any violent action, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I will make this qualification in response to Your Honour's observation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: There was clearly, at the very least, a very strong fear giving rise to specific action on the Muslim side that there would be violent attacks on this bridge beyond sniping. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, but are you asking me that question?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that bridges were being blown up in order to separate the banks from each other, to make it easier to take the right bank of the Neretva where I was, but -- I don't remember this moment, but I think that at that point in time almost all of the bridges had been blown up. Whether the Serbs or the Croats blew them up, well, I don't know exactly. But that pedestrian bridge, not a military one, as was just described by the gentleman a minute ago, the pedestrian called Kamenica in Donja Mahalica [as interpreted] was considered to be a military bridge because we had a location of ours that we were defending. On the other side of the Neretva, there was another company that was defending the harbour. So there was very little communication between the troops on both sides, on both banks. There was the Lucka company guarding the harbour. There were very few troops who crossed that bridge, so my claim is that you can't consider that pedestrian bridge to be a military one.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You have said that there were about 30 to 40 men living in the Donja Mahala area that would guard the area around the clock, protecting themselves again an attack from the HVO, and this bridge was being specifically guarded, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I put it to you, Witness, and this is -- the foundation for this is your own evidence, that what you are saying about sniping activity on this bridge is exaggerated, that you were prepared to take the risk of crossing this bridge and you did take the risk of standing where you stood, where you were shot, precisely because it was not actually sniping activity at that time that was the real concern for you crossing the bridge.

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be quite frank, I haven't understood your question, but I naively believed that a sniper or someone using an ordinary rifle was opening fire on the bridge, and I thought that where I was standing was a safe location. I didn't think I was within the range of a sniper. I thought it was a sufficient end to that alleyway to be quite safe. I quite simply thought that I couldn't be seen at that spot.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Witness, you were in the military, you lived in Mostar, you were standing close to policemen who were sheltering, and yet you stood, only just, but you stood in the open, though according to you, you had dashed across the bridge from pillar to pillar because it was so dangerous. I do put it to you, Witness, that your attempt to say retrospectively that you were foolish, is not really the explanation. It's actually that you are exaggerating the risk from snipers and you are now saying that that was the problem when it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, with due respect, I think you are grossly exaggerating. You want the witness to say something which he obviously does not want to say, because it does not correspond to what he lived. When I asked him quite a while ago what was his fear, he was already weary because he had said so many times that it was fear of sniper. Now, this is the second or the third time that you insist that the witness should say what you want him to say. I do not think that this is a correct behaviour, I'm sorry. It may be in other jurisdictions but --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: -- I think you are losing our time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, it's absolutely correct behaviour, Your Honour, and I do not, with respect, accept a rebuke that it's incorrect behaviour. I am putting the Defence case. If Your Honours are unpersuaded ultimately by any of what we say, you are unpersuaded. But I put my case, I put it professionally, I invite the answers, the witness gives his evidence, we hope truthfully, and that's it, Your Honour. I leave the matter there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, we will move on to another Defence team. Counsel Tomic.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have no questions. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ibrisimovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have no questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We wish to thank the gentleman. We have no questions for the gentleman this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Murphy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. We have no questions for the witness this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours, but could you give the floor to Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Vukotic.

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: I will just go through some technical matters with you to clarify certain things. Could we have document 3D 00756. 0743 is the photograph. 0743, could we have it up? 3D 00756 and then 0743, could we have it up in the screen in the e-court system. And could you please tell me the following: There is one thing that I am trying to clarify here. I think it's also important for the Chamber at the beginning of the conflict when the JNA was still present and the reserve forces, who could have obtained an M48 rifle for example? Was it relatively cheap and easily available, if you had the money?

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know. Perhaps I had enough money to buy such a rifle, I had heard that it was possible to obtain it on the black market, but not through a regular channels.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes, but on the black market, but it was being sold and bought?

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but it's difficult to say that in wartime anything is done in a regular manner.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes, I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, Mr. Praljak asked you a question about the M48 rifle. In Mostar was there a black market which made it possible for one to buy weapons as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had been told that it was possible and that people who had sufficient funds would buy rifles. Perhaps not M48s, but rather more modern rifles and there were quite a few such rifles. Most -- many of them in our company, I don't know how such rifles ended up in our company, but that was the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So as far as you know, it was possible if one had the financial means, to buy weapons, but you said that the weapons that were bought were certainly more modern than the M48, that's what you have just told us. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes. That's logical. It's logical that the men wanted more modern weapons for their own personal defence, or rather whoever had his own weapon --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you were in the 1st company of the 2nd Battalion and were on guard in Donja Mahala, what sort of a weapon did you have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, usually it was an M48. The rifle had different owners. It went from one soldier to the other. It was handed over from one soldier to another, because there were very few rifles available. So when your shift arrived the guard would hand his weapon over to the new shift.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Let's go back to 1992. Who destroyed all the bridges over the Neretva? Apart from the old bridge, who did that?

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, believe me, I'd like to know who was responsible for that. The assumption is that the Serbs destroyed the bridges when the ABiH and the HVO fighting together. The assumption is that the Serbs did that. I wouldn't want to say something that's not correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: In 1992 and 1993, was there constant shelling of Mostar from the Serbian positions?

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to be quite frank, if you want my opinion - my opinion - there was far more shelling from the Croatian side than from the Serbian side.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Mr. Vukotic, that's not something I was claiming. All I wanted to know is whether throughout that period there was shelling from the Serbian positions. I'm not asking you whether one side shelled the town more than another, but was there shelling from those positions?

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: As far as military uniforms are concerned, some people had trousers, some people had jackets, some people didn't have anything. Was it very varied, as I have described it?

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, this question is one that deals with an important issue that the judges will have to decide about. You have just confirmed that during this period of time the Serbs shelled Mostar, the Serbs also shelled Mostar.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are quite certain about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll repeat what I have said, that the ABiH and HVO were allies at the beginning. I will also repeat that most of the shells came from the Serbian side. I myself was on guard in Podvelezje. Not that frequently, that's true, so I could observe the shells flying above our heads, and then out of curiosity we observed Mostar from our positions in order to see where the shells would fall and I can claim that I personally experienced this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will try to be more precise. On the 9th of May, 1993, you know what happened on that date. What I would like to know is what happened after the 9th of May. Did the Serbs shell Mostar after the 9th of May?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, they did. But far less frequently, quite seldom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's take an example at random. When a shell fell at location X in the town, how did one know that the shell came from Serbian positions or Croatian positions or positions held by the ABiH? You, as an inhabitant and as a member of the ABiH, what did you do to establish that the shell had come from such-and-such a location, such-and-such a sector.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A minute ago I said that I was rarely on guard in Podvezelje, and I observed those shells that flew over our heads and hit Mostar. These shells arrived from Serbian positions. As far as shells coming in from the Croatian side are concerned, I was on -- at a location when, for example, the old bridge was targeted from a mountain, from Planinica, I think, and then from Stotina or Abauce [phoen], they shelled the bridge from both sides and I personally saw shells being fired from Croatian positions on that occasion, on such occasions. If I may continue. May I continue?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: You said seldom or not as frequently. Not as frequently in comparison to 1992, but was the shelling from Serbian positions really not as frequent than in 1992? What would you say, Mr. Vukotic?

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, I was seldom on guard in Podvelezje, my colleagues were also on guard in Podvelezje, and that is information that they conveyed to us, to the company when returning from guard duty. What I have seen, I have told you about, what I have heard from others I have also told you about. My conclusion was that there were far more shells from the Croatian side than from the Serbian side. I told you that we had Podvelezje under our control, that is the line between the ABiH and the Serbs. And the each and every shell fired from the Serbian position flew over our heads. You could hear the sound, I mean.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Have a look at this photograph, please. Would you agree with me that it was taken from Stotina?

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: We can see these houses here in the foreground. You have said this was the aluminum company. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure. But I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Very well. Tell me the following: Before the beginning of the war these houses were in a fairly dilapidated state, but had they been fully constructed before the conflict between the Croats and the Muslims broke out?

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not all of them but most of them, yes. May I continue?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Can you point to one that hadn't been fully constructed and to what extent had it been built?

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, look, the third group of the buildings, I don't think it existed then because I know that we were on guard there in those buildings.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Very well. Were they only partially built or did they not exist at all?

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the construction or rough constructions did exist at the time, but whether they had been fully constructed, I can't remember. But they had commenced construction.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Very well. Now, have a look at the photograph and point to the location of the small, suspended bridge, and the location where you were wounded, the entrance to that small alleyway which is vertical to the Neretva. You have a marker so you could mark the photograph with it.

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One comment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This photograph was taken from Stotina, but a little to the left.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. We'll have other photographs too.

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's more to the right, that's my claim, because I think that you can't see the suspended bridge from these positions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Sir, just put number 1 at the location where you think the suspension bridge is and then we will move on to the following photograph. Don't worry, we will do this in a technically correct manner.

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]. Could be here, somewhere here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. Sir, you said something that Mr. Praljak failed to notice, but I did notice it. When we have a look at the buildings in the foreground, I believe that you said that we stood guard in there. Does that mean that the three groups of buildings we have in front of us, your battalion, your company, went on guard duty in these houses, which were still being built? Because others, other people and children who played there, well they said that they played there too. So did you go on guard duty in these houses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We stood guard in all those groups of buildings, even in the first group.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you mark that in with your pencil? Can you show us where you stood guard? Mark the place. You can place an X, for example.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I were at Stotina, I could determine the locality, but this way, from the building I did see Stotina, but I can't say which flat it was. I -- it had been devastated, destroyed, burnt. Because we thought that the enemy would think that there was nobody there. And there was guard duty on the other group of buildings as well, and we were able to monitor the access to the road. And the third group of buildings, which were still under construction, hadn't been completed, was where our third guard post was.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Mr. Vukotic, would you put an A, B, and C where you stood guard in these buildings? So place an A, B, and a C in the three localities, please.

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please. You've just marked the places that you stood guard, and I think that this is something that might have slipped the attention of those who were listening. We see a Bulevar there, so it was the other side. Now, I had the impression that the HVO were not very far from you. Is that right? Is that true or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As the crow flies, well, it would be roughly a distance of -- well, from Stotina and the first buildings, that might be a distance of about 100 metres, roughly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'm just looking at the English transcript, and at line 25 of page 24, that as the crow flies it was about 100 metres. That's very important for me, so I was just checking that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: May I have that same 756 document, 744 is the number of the photograph. 744 is the next number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: To save the image, we need to assign an IC number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, let's have an IC number first, Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will become number IC 376.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What about the initials, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Sir, will you place your initials on the photograph, please. Place your initials.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Praljak likes seeing initials on the document, so put your initials there, please. It's not absolutely necessary, but if it gives you pleasure, then I see no reason why we shouldn't do that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, pleasure or not, I thought it was procedure, Your Honour. If it isn't proceed, I will just move on Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vukotic. Could I have the next document in that series, it is 744. 3D 00756, and then it is 0744. The photograph number is 0744. Here we have it. This is a similar location, Mr. Vukotic; you can see the same line of houses but behind the houses we see the pillars that I think you referred to. The pillars of the suspension bridge. Take a look, and tell me if that is right. And if so, then mark the place where the suspension bridge used to be, and the position at which you were wounded.

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume those are the pillars of the suspension bridge, unless the photograph has been tampered with.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Mr. Vukotic it certainly hasn't been. This photograph was taken two or three days ago, no montage there, no rigging. We see the pillars, there is a path above that.

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a football pitch there, I think. Somewhere there. So if we assume that the pillars belong to the suspension bridge, then it would be over here somewhere, 10 or 12 metres along the river-bank from the right pillar on the left bank of the Neretva River.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Well, could you find that place and put a number 1 there, and number 2 for the pillars, indicating the pillars?

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I put number 2 for both those pillars?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes, a number 2 there. But where were you wounded exactly?

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already marked the spot. I put a number 1.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Put an X as well where you leaned against the wall. You said you leaned against the wall with your right arm, you put one leg forward.

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, perhaps this young lady could see the spot. I can't really find it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Never mind. May we have an IC number for the photograph, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you put your initials on the photograph as well, please? And then we're going to have an IC number.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, this document will become Exhibit IC 377.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, a question comes to mind in looking at this photograph, which shows a lot; it shows the pillars, the place you were wounded, and the buildings in which you stood guard. Now, on the day that you were wounded, that you were hit, I assume that your friends from the 2nd Battalion probably continued to stand guard in those houses, did they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean at that time when I was crossing the bridge, whether they were on duty in the houses there standing guard?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We would stand guard the whole day, although there were less people on duty during the day because they wouldn't attack during the day.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: You mentioned Lucka, Luka and Lucki most or Luka bridge, and this area and where the Lucka company was. So could you indicate the area referred to as Luka and the Lucki bridge as well, and you can put a number 3 there.

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As an inhabitant of Mostar, looking at this area from the north, it begins with Lucki bridge and stretches roughly to the new bridge, or Hasan Brkic bridge, as it's called, and we can't see that on the photograph.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: All right. Then just draw a circle.

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm going to put an arrow to show you the direction.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes, draw a big arrow. You don't have to save on the paper and pen. And the photograph will be clearer and you will save perhaps me or somebody else if you draw in a bold arrow so we can see it. And draw a bold circle around the Luka area and the Lucki bridge.

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this is Luka and that's Lucki bridge.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Right. Put a number 3 there, and that will do it. Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Vukotic. Next photograph please, 745. To make the geography of the region even clearer --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we have an IC number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be IC 378.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]. I'd like the next photograph on our screens now, 745. It's from the same set. That's the next photograph, yes. Here we have it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: It's a close-up view. Now we can see it all clearly. We see the houses up in front, we know what they were used for and what they looked like. And then we see three pillars. We see a sports pitch there, sports ground, and we can see a bridge, which is the Lucki bridge. Now, is what I have said correct? If so, put a 1 by the pillars, a 2 by the football pitch, and a number 3, the spot where you were standing when you were wounded, when you were hit.

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You want me to mark the pillars first, do you, with a number 1?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And then the spot where I was wounded? I can't see the spot. I can't see the spot because -- well, the bridge isn't there anymore.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes, but you can see the pillars, so could you put an arrow in the general direction of where you were wounded?

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't want to do that because you might use it against me in times to come.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Mr. Vukotic, of course not. Put a number 2 and then a question mark. Maybe it was there, maybe it wasn't. Mr. Vukotic, after your testimony, we're going to have an expert witness come into court and I assume, I suppose, he managed to indicate the exact spot. So put a number 3 by the bridge, the bridge we can see there?

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Lucki bridge, you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes, Lucki bridge.

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: And your initials, please, and let's move on.

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] An IC number, Mr. Registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, this document will become IC 379.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While we are trying to find these photographs, it's all a rather slow process, can we have an IC number?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: At Stotina, let me ask you that, the HVO soldiers were at Stotina?

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I suppose you know that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes, but I'm asking you. Do you agree with me that the HVO soldiers were at Stotina?

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, I'm certain that it couldn't have been the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Tell me now, please, how long that bridge of yours that we can see quite nicely from Stotina, how long it was functioning as a pedestrian bridge, and as a bridge across which the soldiers crossed and civilians crossed, and food was taken across the bridge. How long was that bridge standing, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, I'm happy to have met you, however I'm not quite clear on what you are asking me. You keep saying that the bridge was a military facility used for -- by soldiers and to transport food to the other bank. I don't agree with you there. Perhaps it was, but I don't think it was used for that purpose. That's my first comment. That is what you are telling me, but I --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: It's enough for one soldier to cross a bridge and the bridge becomes a military target. Now my next question is this: Now, this bridge number 3, had that been destroyed during the war? Was it standing at the time?

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Tell me now, why, if there was a better bridge, another bridge, a safer and firmer bridge, why did you risk your life to cross a bridge and run the risk of being shot at when there was another bridge? Now wasn't it logical that a bridge was used to transport food to soldiers, to carry any wounded people and things like that? That was logical, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I answer that? On what basis do you claim that on the left bank of the Neretva there was a food factory for us? Why don't you say that we had logistics or rather that we had our families our -- our parents who fed us? Why would we need to get food from the other side? You just said that food was carried across the bridge, transported across.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: No, Mr. Vukotic, I didn't mention any food factory or anything like that. That just didn't exist.

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but if food was transported then the food must have been made somewhere.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: All I'm asking you is whether food had to reach an enclave, if not every day, at least once a fortnight. Some food had to come in. If bread was baked, then you needed flour. And flour needed to be transported.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Tell me this: How long was that bridge standing there to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: All right. If you were a commander and you wanted to blow the place up and you placed a tank at Stotina with a ZIS, a tank, or any other weapon, was it possible to destroy that bridge in five minutes or in the morning or during the day or at dusk or twilight or whatever? Is it an easy job? Is it easy to blow up a bridge? What do you think, you personally?

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'll tell you. That was a conundrum for us too.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Right. A conundrum. Now, can we put this up on the overhead projector? We're getting through this rather slowly. I don't want to try the man's patience. I just want to have a look at two or three other things and we will be finished quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, Mr. Praljak, there is a question from the Bench.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, while we are waiting for the document come up on the overhead projector. Mr. Praljak seems to have shown you another route that you could have taken, the big bridge that we see on the photograph. Now, my question for you is this: When you were the object of the shooting, this big bridge was the -- did the bridge come under fire from snipers? Was the bridge sniped at as well? Was that a dangerous bridge too? Was it as dangerous to cross the big bridge as the small one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that bridge did not exist; it had been destroyed. You couldn't cross that bridge because allegedly the Serbs had blown it up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's what I understood. That's how I understood it. So you seem to have been a little hesitant in asking Mr. Praljak's questions. Now, without being -- we see Luka and Donja Mahala and how they are connected, and we know that there is a front-line there between the ABiH and the HVO. And you said a moment ago that you were standing guard in the buildings at Donja Mahala. And we could assume that the BH Army was deployed in-depth in that zone. And so that is perhaps why the bridge was of strategic importance, because it linked the two banks. And everybody who has done their military service in the army knows that there are logistical problems, and that these soldiers need to have supplies coming in, whether they be food supplies or military materiel, or weapons, or whatever, other supplies. So someone of medium intelligence could perhaps think that people were walking across the bridge bringing in logistical support to the BH Army. That was deployed opposite the front-line. So my question to you is a very simple one: To your knowledge, to the best of your knowledge, on this little bridge with the pillars, and we only see the pillars standing now, did you ever see any of your colleagues, BH Army soldiers, transporting food, weapons, or other resources and material? You see, it's quite clear.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, look, given the situation, the sniper fire, everyone moved around as little as possible. Only when it was really necessary, so there was no need for me to go there to observe anything. I would just go to the guard post, to the command, and home. And that was the case for everyone else because of the shelling, because of sniper fire, and so on. Movement was limited, everyone limited their movements. I can't remember having crossed over that bridge at the time of the war apart from on that occasion, on that one occasion. So I had never been to that bridge before, and was not able to observe what you have been referring to. Now, in terms -- I apologise, but if I may continue, I would like to answer Mr. Praljak's question, I have remembered something in the meantime. I don't know what sort of weapons he listed to -- that could be used to fire on the bridge, but does he think one could climb up to Stotina without this being noticed on the side of Luka? They could have gone to the top of Stotina with a ZIS or a tank, but that would have been dangerous because it would have been possible to open fire on those objects from Luka.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes, naturally, the 4th Corps had its artillery on Luka and they could have prevented that but we'll deal with that later. But that bridge wasn't destroyed, but let's have a look at the first photograph on the ELMO now. You can see a man standing on Stotina, in front of a house that you will see later on. What you can see in the background, is that Mostar, photographed from Stotina? You see that?

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not right now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Have a look at the mosque, these houses, you can see that this photograph was taken from Stotina, that you can see the bridge in the distance.

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I knew Stotina very well, as a child I used to play ball there, it was a playground. But this is a black and white photograph.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Can you see the buildings to the left, can you recognise a single building, can you recognise the mosque to the left?

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see it, but I don't know which mosque it is.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: The mosque in Donja Mahala.

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The mosque in Donja Mahala. When was this photograph taken?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Two days ago.

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why isn't it in colour? I really can't say whether this is taken from Stotina. If it was in colour, it would be easier for me to find my bearings.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Can you now see that this is Stotina? We have zoomed in. Can you see that this was taken from Stotina?

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't see some buildings to the right.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: They are down below, but in front of the mosque can you see these two buildings?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, Witness, I haven't been on the Stotina hill, but apparently there are certain objects that permit identification, there is the minaret, and this might lead one to belief this was taken from Stotina. You played football there, you were an inhabitant, you were on guard. Are you telling us you don't recognise this photograph.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have told you I was on Stotina 30 or 40 years ago and Stotina has changed since that time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Let me help you, Witness. Do you know the street that goes from this mosque by these two buildings that you can see here? The street that is called Gojka Vukovica street, can you see these two Sokol buildings in the Gojka Vukovica street, just by the minaret?

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see one building and some kind of a fir tree, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: But we have zoomed in, so these buildings seem to be close to each other, but do you recognise this building as a building in Gojko Vukovica street?

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's where I live, but I can't see my house. I lived to the left of the Sokol buildings but I can't see it because of the obstacles. Why are you asking me whether this is a view from Stotina. If you know, if this is the mosque in Donja Mahala, then my house is by the Sokol building to the left of the house. If you saying this is a view from Stotina, then why are you maltreating me? If that is the case, then that is the case. The coloured photograph, yes, I don't know about the other one.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Mr. Vukotic, you agreed to testify, if the judges could solve the problem through me, they would interrogate me, examine me, and we would have solved the problem. Witnesses come here to help the Judges by working with the Prosecution and the Defence in order for us to establish something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, put your question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Was this photograph taken of Stotina, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Let's move on. Let's have a look at the next photograph. These are the legs of this man. Do you recognise the photograph as having been taken from Stotina now?

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, where are the two Sokol buildings? You should have the one next to the other.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you see the Luka bridge in the distance?

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, if that is the Luka bridge.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: You can see that there are two buildings there --

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: There are photographs of these on e-court, if that would help the Court. They are in colour, not in black and white.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Put the last one up on the screen, the one in colour. Could we have a look at the next photograph? Let's have the last one. That's the one. Just the one in colour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Has this photograph been taken from Stotina?

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Put your initials on it and could you mark the location of your house with the number 1 and an arrow, approximately?

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]. May I continue?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Mark the location of the pillars where the bridge was with number 2.

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. Could we have an IC number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] An IC number.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And your initials, Mr. Vukotic, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will become IC 380.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to say something for the transcript. In this photograph I can note that there is an individual in the photograph, and at the level of the individual one can see the bridge that was destroyed and the location where the witness was when he was wounded by a projectile. From this view-point this can be seen very clearly. I wanted to say this for the sake of the transcript. Mr. Praljak, do continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]. Could we have the next photograph in colour. The one on the ELMO represents a building in Stotina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have we had an IC number? Very well then, let's move on to the next photograph.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's sufficient to place it on the ELMO. We're just interested in the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Your Honours may I just interrupt Mr. Praljak for one moment to inquire what his line of questioning is because as I see it, he is just presenting a photograph and asking the witness if he recognises certain buildings in it and then he moves on to the next photograph. I'm not certain that this is advancing the case or assisting the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but I assume that he will put a question that will enlighten the Judges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: May I have a follow-up question? The -- Mr. Flynn the -- asked Mr. Praljak really to ask a question from the witness, and Mr. Praljak has asked his -- has started his questioning actually 10 to 3.00, so it is now more than 45 minutes, and it is really quite a good time to -- to listen to his questions. I have been following his questions very carefully, and I was pleased to know more about Mostar, and about the bridges, and about important questions. I am sure of that. On the other hand, really, I am afraid that we have been losing great kind of good time for this, so I also would like to ask Mr. Praljak to proceed with his question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, put your question that is more the result of what you have been demonstrating so that your procedure can be a useful one. Otherwise the Judges will say, Yes, we've seen Stotina, the view from Stotina, the location where the witness was wounded, but it's necessary for you to tie up everything that you have been demonstrating by putting a clear question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll see another photograph of a building from which allegedly a sniper opened fire.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: My question is: If on the sketch that we had a look at we saw the angle of the street that descended to the Neretva River and in we saw the way in which Mr. Vukotic was leaning against the wall, then it's more than clear for anyone who has any notion of Euclidean geometry that the entry/exit wound to the leg, the wound that penetrated the leg from the back is not a wound that can be inflicted if fire is opened from Stotina. This is something we will determine through the expert witness. My question is as follows: Mr. Vukotic when you have a look at this photograph, you leave the bridge, you lean against the wall as you demonstrated for the benefit of the Prosecution, and now you see Stotina before you, but -- and please try to use your imagination. Is it possible, if your back it turned to Neretva and you are facing Luka, is it possible for a bullet to arrive from this point, this view-point, to penetrate the back of your knee and exit at a right angle? No one disputes the fact that you were wounded, but the bullet that hit you, could it have been fired from this location? No one disputes the fact that you were wounded, but given the way or the position in which you were standing, could this bullet have been fired from Stotina? You know, you don't know, or you can't say?

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I apologise I am an economist. If you asked me what five times five is, I could answer that question. If you ask me what angle the bullet could have hit me at and whether my leg was to the left or right of the Neretva bank, well, I really couldn't say, sir. Don't address this question to me, you should address this question to the expert.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. The entire demonstration was done for it the sake of this question, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: According to your information, is this the building in Stotina from which the notorious sniper opened fire?

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well how would I know which house the sniper opened fire from? If someone had seen him from Donja Mahala, he probably would have opened fire on him. How am I to know? All these holes on this building, I don't know whether these three windows are facing Donja Mahala or somewhere else, but these HVO soldiers also made such holes in order to open sniper fire through those holes. This was done deliberately.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: They have some windows. Why would they make any holes?

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to deceive others, I'm not that naive. Naturally he's not going to use a window, because he is visible there. He will use a hole. We did that too.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So you did that too. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours, for your patience; unfortunately, I had to proceed in this way because it was important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I think all the Defence teams have completed their cross-examinations. Would the Prosecution perhaps have an additional question or two.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: No, Your Honours have covered anything that I might have had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Vukotic, on behalf of my colleagues I would like to thank you for having come to The Hague and for having answered all the questions put to you. Perhaps certain questions were a little difficult for you to understand, but you should know that the Judges need to obtain certain answers to very legitimate questions that one has to ask in such situations. I do thank you. I wish you a safe trip home, and I will now ask the usher to escort you out of the courtroom. It's now 20 to 4.00, we will have a 20-minute break and we will resume our hearing and we will be calling the expert witness into the courtroom after the break. I think we will have sufficient time for the Prosecution to conduct its examination-in-chief of this witness, and tomorrow we can start with the cross-examination. So we will resume at 5 past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We resume. Sir, would you stand, please? Sir, would you stand, please, because you're going to take the solemn declaration. For the transcript, you are going to give us your name, surname and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Patrick van der Weijden. My date of birth is the 26th of September, 1971.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And what is your current occupation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am a Dutch Army officer in the Dutch special forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What rank? Captain?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am a first lieutenant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. Lieutenant, have you ever testified in a court of law about the events that took place in Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1992, 1993, and 1994, or is this the first time that you are testifying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the first time I am testifying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Would you now go ahead and read the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may be seated. Some explanation from me to start off with. This is the first time you are in a court of law. You are going to start off by answering questions put to you by the Prosecution, will be based on a written report compiled by you, and it refers to sniping. After that first stage, which should last about two hours, the Prosecution have two hours, perhaps the bench will have some questions to ask you. You will see that I have a number of highly technical questions to ask you, but anyway we will finish the day according to that schedule. Tomorrow it will be the turn of the Defence. There seem to be a lot of Defence counsel, but one counsel will be representing each of the accused, and that is the cross-examination stage. And almost certainly seeing as we're dealing with highly technical matters, the accused will probably have questions to ask you as well, because the Trial Chamber has given the accused the right to ask questions themselves. So you will therefore be answering their questions too. So that, in general terms, is how the proceedings will evolve. As we're going to have very highly technical questions to ask you, try and be as specific and clear as possible, and you must start out from assuming that the Judges only have rudimentary knowledge in the area of arms, of weapons. So your answers should explain things to us. Of course, your written report has already cleared up a lot of facts and points, and I have consulted your report ten times so far and found it very helpful. So that in general terms is how the proceedings will evolve. Without losing any more time, because time is of the essence and very precious, I am going to give the floor, without further ado, to the Prosecution to start off with the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Lieutenant van der Weijden. As I mentioned yesterday, we need to pause between question and answer so that the interpreters and the court reporters can follow us. Do you understand that sir?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let's start off if you can briefly tell the Trial Chamber about your military career from the time you joined the Dutch Army to the present.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: I was -- I entered the Dutch Army in 1991, 1990, as a conscript and a group sergeant in the mechanised infantry. I left the army for two years, returned to the army as a private in the Dutch air mobile brigade as a sharpshooter. In 1995 I joined the Dutch special forces, again as a sharpshooter, and later received my training as a sniper. And I joined -- entered the Dutch special forces, I enter as a corporal. After two years I went to military school to become a non-commissioned officer and got my officer commission in 1999, January.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Lieutenant, I will stop you there. In English I noticed the word sharpshooter. Is there a difference between an elite shooter and a sniper? Is it the same idea, or is there a difference?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There is a difference. A sharpshooter is common in most infantry units, and a sharpshooter is usually a soldier within an infantry unit, whereas a slightly better rifle than the rest of his squad, but is still operating within that squad, so he still receives his order from a team or group commander.
