The sniper is different, that he can operate alone of -- at least in a two-man team. He is -- he is -- he is also of course a sharpshooter because he is trained for long-range shooting, but he gets an additional technical training which allows him to operate with two or three people, operate independently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We have made significant progress.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Lieutenant van der Weijden, would you tell the Trial Chamber about the types and levels of military training you have received since rejoining the Dutch Army in the early 1990s?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: The first military training I received when re-entering was, of course, the basic military training and advance military training for an air mobile brigade. In addition I received my individual specialism as a sharpshooter at a sharpshooter course given by the Dutch Army. When transferring to the Dutch special forces after completing our selection course, I got into advanced special forces training, which includes my specialty as a sniper. I further on during my career, apart from the career courses, such as the military school and the military academy, I received an advanced sniper training in urban environment but that's a training and courses as a firearms instructor, given by the Dutch police, police academy, as well as the sniper instructor course given by our unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And a follow-up question from what you have just said. To your knowledge, in the NATO-member states, as you said, is there any special training to be a sniper?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To my experience most armies I have trained with or operated alongside with do have sniper units or snipers employed in their army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us, lieutenant, what are the specific subjects that were taught at the sniping course that you have attended?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: The main subjects that are taught in the sniper course is the sniper theory, which gives the sniper background as to what the sniper and what his tasks are in operations. The practical subjects are shooting, of course, at longer ranges under various conditions. The tactical training is made up of stalking, which is getting closer to the target without being seen, and there are several other subjects that allow him to do that, and those are camouflage and concealment, which is a sort of stationary training where you have to take in fire position unseen and be able to observe the target. In addition, another one is judging distance, which allows you to judge the distance correctly without the use of laser range finders, by formulas or just experience. And those are the main subjects of the sniper course. And before I forget, one is observation. Observation is very important for the snipers. It's the skill that allows him to detect, identify, and observe the enemy or the target.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, you also mentioned that you attend a sniper trainer's course. Can you tell us what you learned at that training course?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: The sniper instructor course runs parallel to the sniper course given at my unit. It is -- the course trains you to set up a sniper course for other snipers so that you have to plan, stalk which can -- the trainees can execute. You have to plan and set up observation ranges. Yeah, that is the type of training you receive at the sniper instructor course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Lieutenant van der Weijden did you successfully complete --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, may I add a question on the training? Are snipers also trained in identifying objects and in limits as to the legitimacy of their engagement? Are they told you can shoot at such-and-such a target but not at others?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The snipers are taught that -- the sniper courses that I am familiar with are taught about identification in so far that you have to identify certain objects which are usually military objects. The identification or the legal side of it, so what can the sniper shoot and what not depends on the rules of engagement he receives in a conflict. But are not discussed in the sniper course itself, but are discussed prior to deployment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Can you specify what you mean when you say "usually military targets"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, usually military, the objects that are used in the observation ranges during the sniper course could be military objects, also rifle magazine, water bottles, shovels, just any military type of equipment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's go to the heart of the matter straight away because everything you say is very important. But could you very quickly tell us, as far as you are able, within the Dutch Army training and I think that it -- the same applies to NATO, what does a sniper have the right to do and not to do? Can he snipe at a tank, a house inhabited by a civilian, or perhaps a civilian walking? Can you, in general terms, tell us what a sniper is entitled to do and what he is not entitled to do, based on the rules of engagement as taught to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I -- as I have said before, it's the rules of engagement depend on the type of deployment. A peacekeeping mission will have different rules of engagement than a police enforcement mission or a regular conflict, but in general the rules of engagement that I have received during my deployments included the threat to own personnel. If there was a threat to our own personnel, you could use appropriate force, or if there was a threat to the civilian population, you were also allowed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What we are mainly interested in are the rules of engagement that govern an armed conflict. We are not talking about a -- law and order. What can a sniper do in a wartime situation?

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour just so we're clear --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Murphy, let the witness answer the question and you will have sufficient time, unless there is an error in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would just like to ask, just for clarification, if Your Honour is asking the witness for a legal opinion, whether Your Honour's question is directed to the practice of the Dutch Army. Just what the parameters are so that the record is clear as to what the witness's opinion is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Murphy, if you are following what I was saying, and as I know that you know French, that's the case for the witness too, I asked what the rules of engagement were. The rules of engagement that he was taught during his training, and the question was quite precise, what sort of training did he have. So my question is, what were you taught in conflict situations, or when you were in a conflict situation, if your country is at war with another country, your country is country A and you are a sniper of country A engaged in a war against country B. What could you do, how could you act as a sniper. What were you not allowed to do, what would you not be allowed to do? According to what you were taught, I'm not asking you about the law, I'm asking you what you were told, what sort of margin for manoeuvre you had in the field.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were told not to engage civilian targets, unless the civilian targets were actively participating in a, you know, threatening role. So if they were using weapons then they were not -- were not to be considered civilian anymore, but a combatant, part of the warring factions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So that was a general principle that you were taught.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Lieutenant let me just ask you about one other training course that you attended. You mentioned before the police academy that you attended. Can you tell us what you were taught at the police academy and particularly the subjects that were relevant to producing the report that you have produced for us here.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: There are a lot of similarities between the police arms instructor course compared to the sniper instructor course. Both cover shooting training, so how to plan exercises for -- for trainees to become better shooters than they usually are. Apart from that, we got subjects we were trained on ballistics, how weapons are made up, how weapons operate, how they -- and on the ballistics we received the lessons in how bullets behave when they enter a soft tissue like human tissue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Other than that last subject matter, the effects of bullet when they enter soft tissue, have you had, sir, any medical training whatsoever?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: We do at my unit receive specialised medical training in which we are shown wounds, bullet wounds on slides, so not live because that's reserved for our medical personnel. But we do receive training as to how bullet wounds, what they look like, what's an entry wound, what's an exit wound and also what happens in the body when -- what a bullet does within the human body.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Lieutenant van der Weijden I'd now like to move on to another topic, which is sniping in general, if you will. There is a section in your report where you talk about laypersons' perceptions of sniping. Can you briefly tell us about that part of your report?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: In my experience there is a lot of difference between the military sniper as trained in most western armies and the sniper as is portrayed usually in the media. The military sniper is a professional who acts within strict rules of engagement and who is considered a valuable tool on the battlefield because he is able to surgically take out targets without the risk of collateral damage. The media sniper, if I might call it like that, is just of usually an unseen gunman that shoots at whatever he sees. Examples of that are the Washington Sniper, as a couple -- for what happened a couple of years ago, who wasn't a sniper but with a rifle. He did have a scope, so there are some similarities. But it's different, there are a lot of differences.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let's turn, sir, to the military use of the sniper. Can you tell us what the functions and specific missions or taskings that are typically given by militaries to sniper teams?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: The main task of the sniper as is given, as are used in the NATO armies are the neutralising of enemy personnel in the order of other snipers or enemy snipers, enemy commanding personnel communication specialists, cruiser weapons and command and control structures. So they can be used in anti-materiel role as well. Apart from that, intelligence gathering, covert intelligence gathering, by observation, advice to higher commands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Lieutenant, we're going into technical details more and more, and we're beginning to deal with rather complicated issues. I would like what you say to be very clear. You said that you were part of a special forces unit. And my question is: A sniper within a special forces unit, is such a sniper identical to a sniper in a classical military unit or is a special forces sniper a sniper of a different kind? Does he have different sort of training, a different weapon, different -- a different technique that he employs or is there absolutely no difference?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There are differences between the snipers in special forces operations or special forces and regular infantry units. The tasks of the sniper that I've written down in the report are the task of the general sniper, sniper in general, which are also applicable in regular units. In addition, special forces snipers are by their nature, able to operate more independently and behind enemy lines and -- but usually are used in support of direct action operations, so a raid on a -- on -- yeah, compound, in support of the assault element.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as equipment is concerned, does a special forces sniper who is in the enemy's depth has -- have equipment that is different from that used by traditional units in the field? If I just refer to the special forces, American in Vietnam, as far as I know they had equipment that was different from the equipment used by regular units. Could you provide us with some information on these technical details? A minute ago I told you that we would be dealing with technical issues, and here is the proof.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There are differences between -- in the equipment of special forces units and regular units. In the Dutch Army and in most NATO countries, actually, snipers in special forces units and the regular unit have the same type of position rifle, so the same type of sniper rifles, but special forces units in addition to have access to extra sniper rifles. So maybe, for instance, suppressed rifles, which allow a sniper to silently take down his target, or anti-materiel rifles which are larger calibre, just to give special force teams which usually operate on -- with a small amount of people, some extra power. But the basic sniper rifle is usually the same as in regular infantry units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And to finish this question and also links up to a concern we had when a witness testified here, in the case of special forces with a certain type of weapon, for example in Vietnam, who didn't have an M16, they had a colt commando 15, which is a smaller weapon than the M16, well, I'm interested in the flash at the time that the shot is fired. When the ball exits the weapon of special forces sniper or some other sniper, is there materiel that one can use, equipment that can be used to conceal the flash when the shot is fired?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There are two ways to low -- to diminish the amount of flash visible at the time of firing. The first one is the flash Hider which is used on two rifles in the report, which is the Dragunov and the M76. They do have a flash hider. It's a small metal addition at the end of the barrel, with some -- some holes which allow the flame to disintegrate in smaller flames, which makes it less -- less visible. The other way to hide the flash would be to use the use of a suppressor, which also diminishes the sound of the -- of the shot. And that absorbs the flame of the -- the flash of the shot within the suppressor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So a weapon that didn't have these two devices, if it was used to fire a bullet, did that mean that the flame coming out of the barrel is visible in daylight at a certain distance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In sniper training you also receive training in how to -- because you have to approach the target and then shoot at the target, but you also have to get away unseen of course for your own protection. So there are ways in choosing your position, in which a flash would be less visible. The bigger concern for the sniper is not the flash but it is more the smoke that can be generated if the -- the rifle has not been clean enough and there is some oil remnants within the barrel. That's a bigger problem for the sniper than the flash itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Lieutenant, I just have one question that concerns the difference between a sharpshooter and a special forces sniper. Can a difference be made on the basis of the distance between them and their target? In other words, what's the greatest possible distance that one could have between the shooter and the target, and is there a difference as far as this distance is concerned when it comes to these three categories of shooters?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We apologise, Mr. Mundis, if you wanted to put these questions. But as you can see the judges are so impatient to go to the heart of the matter that we are already dealing with these very technical details.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The differences would be that the sharpshooter would have -- in most armies has a slightly different weapon. He has the same rifle as the rest of his squad, but in addition he has a small scope on it or a rifle sight, optical sight. Which allows him to strike out a little farther than the rest of his squad, and the sniper in regular units, in western armies has a bolt-action rifle which is a manually operated rifle. Every time you shoot around you want to shoot again, you will have to manually operate the rifle, pull it back, feed a new round into the chamber, put the wire bolt forward, and then you will be able to fire again. Most sharp shooters employ semi-automatic weapons that do that automatically but have a mechanism within the trigger group which does not allow them to fire automatically. So there is, on the distances, it depends on the weapon system, it depends on the experience and the qualities of the shooter so that it's different to say if -- but if I would say a sniper with the same weapon as a sharpshooter, they would be able to strike out at the same distance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My colleague asked you to inform us of the approximate distances. So that we could have an idea without going into all the details, because we certainly will go into the details during the course of your cross-examination. But roughly speaking what is an average distance, what is the minimum distance, what was the greatest possible distance.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The closest distance, of course, is -- well, depending how far the target would be from the shooter. It can be very close. If you look at police snipers, the average distance for police snipers usually is 25 metres, so that's really close.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly slow down, Witness, please, for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry. For military snipers would usually in western armies with the ammunition that is used there, which is slightly similar to the rounds that I've described in the report, the distance for -- the maximum distance for a trainee to be able to hit a target would be 800 metres and harassing fire, which is maybe hitting the target but at least stopping him from doing what he was doing, would be 1.000 metres. But the -- the maximum distance, there are records as early as in Vietnam of 2500 metres. So depending on the calibre, it can be a very long distance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And to conclude with this issue, I think we've made much progress already. Depending on the distance one might assume that the sight on the weapon plays a role. According to the literature, it seems that the sight is X 4, X 6, X 10, times four, times six, times ten. So the field of vision one has through the scope, if one has an M82, for example, can one fire at a very long range?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is possible to fire with -- even with a 10 times magnification, to fire at over two kilometres. The chances would diminish, of course, because of 10 times magnification, but it is possible as long as the quality of the optic is good.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you briefly, Lieutenant van der Weijden tell us about the methods or the methodology that snipers employ in carrying out their missions?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: It would be -- the difference -- I will split them into static -- static operations and -- or offensive operations. In offensive operations a sniper would be given a target or an area on a map which he -- which he would have to cover. He will do a map study, identify ways to approach the target to get within a distance, within shooting distance. Then with his spotter, who is a colleague sniper, but he is -- who is equipped with usually optical equipment of a larger magnification such as a 20 times magnification then with a team they will be inserted by tracked vehicle, wheeled vehicle or on foot, ask they will infiltrate, make their way into a sniper height or a position where they can keep their presence up for the time asked for in the order, and they will set up their operations and wait for the target to appear to take out the target. In static operations, in a defensive environment, they could be asked to occupy one position, map out or draw out range cards, which is a card they draw out, what they see in front of them, houses, trees, measure out the distances to the houses or trees so that when they have to fire they can quickly determine what range it is so they can fire at their targets, which takes, yeah, usually about a couple of hours to -- nowadays with laser range finders to correctly draw out the cards. So there is -- for static operations there is less preparation necessary than for offensive operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You have mentioned sir laser range finders. Would you be able to draw out or map out, produce range cards without laser range finders? And if so, how would you do that?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Laser range finders have only been around since the mid-1990s and then in small numbers. They're pretty common right now at this time, and most sniper teams are equipped with laser range finders. But prior to laser range finders the more conventional methods were taught and so that judging distance, there are some -- you can, of course, first just on the map identify your own position and with the use of built-up areas so you can identify a house, try to locate on the map, just measure out the distance, that would be one way, the easiest way. Another way to be to compare -- comparative method is to pick yourself, in your mind, football fields, if you are an active footballer, you will know about -- just about at what distance a football field would be in the field and then multiply the number of fields it would be until the target. That's the comparative. Then you have a method, if the person's arms would be visible, it would -- the person would be at 100 metres, if he would be just -- just a silhouette, you wouldn't see any extremities, he would be at 200 metres, just the way of appearance. But one of the most accurate methods is there is -- the use of a formula, and with the use of the optical equipment. But I would have to draw out that to -- to make it obvious because it is very difficult to explain just verbally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you this, sir: If there are ways -- you have talked a number of times about distinguishing targets and distinguishing targets. Are there ways that you can acquire the skills of how to make such distinctions and if so, how do you do that?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Well, I think the quality of the -- the ability to distinguish people from -- from one another is a quality that everyone has, except a sniper might be able to do it at longer ranges because of training or experience. As I have written in the report, a child compared to an adult, if they were walking in front of a house at 500 metres, you would -- and there was a doorway, the child wouldn't come up -- wouldn't be -- would only come up to halfway the door, so that would easily identify -- be identifiable as a child instead of an adult, who would come up to three quarters of the doorway. So that would be one way to distinguish. The other way would be for combatants, non-combatants, camouflage uniforms, colourful clothing, hairstyles, their actions, what they are doing. If people are playing football, in combination of the way they move. Because older people move differently because of the bone structure -- yeah, young people, just normal observations, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Lieutenant van der Weijden, now you have talked about these various training courses that you have attended. Would it be possible to acquire many of these same kinds of skills without undergoing this type of training?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: I do think so. If -- especially on shooting, if you would have a hunting background, in hunting a lot of the skills used in sniper courses, they come from hunting. The stalking, the term itself comes from stalking the prey or just getting close to the prey you want to shoot. The Ghillie suit, the camouflage equipment that we use as snipers is traditionally a Scottish gamekeepers' uniform, so that it is -- there are a lot of similarities between hunting and sniping. The -- a hunter would also be to get close to its prey because animals have a -- more acute senses, so if they detect people nearby, they will try to get away. So it will be very important to get close to the animal unseen. And also if an animal is not hit at the right spot, he will run away and die later out of your sight, so you wouldn't have the -- the meat, if you wanted to eat the animal. So it would be very important to hit the target at the right spot, which would mean that you would have to correctly judge the distance and know where to shoot at the animal. So there is a lot of similarities between sniping and hunting. An observation, I think, I guess in my opinion, just regular observation of people would give someone the ability to distinguish people from combatant or civilian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, can you tell us again, let's switch back to the -- a situation where there is a sniping training regimen, if you will, or sniping courses. What level of skill would a shooter have to have in order to be either selected for or to successfully pass, and again a western or NATO-type sniping course?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Well, the shooter would have -- the trainee would have to be able to hit the target with consecutive shots at almost the same -- he would have to be able to get a group on the target at almost the same spot. So even if he might be able to hit a target once, at exactly the right spot, but would not be able to hit the target several times at the same spot, that would make him less suitable instead -- compared to the shooter who is not hitting the target at exactly the right spot but is able to hit the target at that spot where he first hit for several times. So shooting skills is of course important. But otherwise from that he would have to be responsible, because he would operate alone or with a very small team. He would have to be intelligent, he would have to be physically fit, good eyesight. Although with good optical equipment, sometimes glasses would not be that big of a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: But just so that we're clear, sir, it's not possible to take a typical infantry company and turn every one of them into a sniper?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: No, because most people don't have the shooting skills to hit targets at longer ranges, even with precision rifles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question concerns the current situation rather than 1993 but, when training, are there psychological test that is allow one to establish what the right psychological profile for a sniper would be, I'm talking in particular to self-control, to morale, to those sort of things. Are there well-developed tests for this category of combatants?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For my unit we would already have a high filter just to the unit, so we don't have additional psychological training for becoming a sniper within my unit, and within the Dutch Army people are usually tested psychologically to be able to operate under stress. And if they are not able to operate under stress to a high degree, they would not be placed at a responsible position, so they wouldn't be made a group commander or a platoon commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, Lieutenant, I'd like to turn now to a new topic. Can you tell us, sir, in taking on this project to produce your report, what were the instructions that you were provided? What were you told to do in producing this report?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: From the ICTY I received of -- the minister of defence receives a request for support in this investigation. Through my unit they asked me if I could help them. I was asked to take a look at several incidents and try to determine if the position that the witnesses gave as the possible shooting location, if that was possible. If it was possible, at what range would the shooting location would have been. For what type of rifle would have been used, and if there were would be any other options of course, if it would be the only position that the shots were fired from, or would there be more possibilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And in order to produce your report, sir, what materials were you provided with by the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Well, I have them with me. I was provided with photographs of some of the scars of the victims to try to determine what kind of ammunition or rifles were used. I was provided with the medical reports as well as death certificates of the victims. And with some -- a map of Mostar, some photographs of Mostar, and two cities, one with witness interviews and one with 360 presentation of Mostar, which included all the locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, Lieutenant van der Weijden, when you say witness interviews, can you tell us what that was, the video with the witness interviews, what was the gist of those witness interviews that you have referred to?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: On the witness interviews there was the investigator Carry Spork, who was in contact with at the location where the incident happened, asked the witnesses or victims to point out where the exact location was where they were shot at, what they believed -- what their actions were at the time, if they were -- if they were aware where they were fired on, from where they were fired on. Just in general the -- try to -- the description of the incidents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One word, sir. You didn't go to Mostar, you didn't visit the sites?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, in addition that's the instructions I received, on the DVDs. After receiving the basic information, so the -- the photographs and the witness reports, for me it would have been -- it was very helpful to be able to go to Mostar, to visit the sites, and also to visit the alleged shooting locations to try to determine if it would be possible to fire from those locations at the incident sites. So I did go to Mostar for three days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You went with Mr. Carry Spork, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I travelled along to Sarajevo, I was picked up by Mr. Spork, accompanied -- together with a interpreter, a local interpreter of the Sarajevo field office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And did you meet any of the victims there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't meet any of the victims. I did meet -- well, meet, I saw a witness in case number 3, he was the husband who found his wife on the terrace. He had to open his door for me to take a look at the terrace. So I didn't talk to him directly but I did see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, Lieutenant van der Weijden, do you recall whether you were provided with any written statements of any of the witnesses to read?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: I wasn't provided with any written statement. The only description of the incident, apart from the video of the -- the DVD compilation, was a summary of the incidents with the GPS coordinates of the incident, just a quick description of the incident itself. I didn't get the names of the victims. And there was also the alleged shooting location on that summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, sir, can you tell us, did you at any point in time read any of the trial transcripts or watch any of the trial testimony, either live or on the internet or on DVD, of any of the witnesses who have testified in this case?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: No, I have not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, Judge Antonetti a few moments ago asked you about your mission to Mostar. Can you just -- and I'm going to go through each of the incidents in the report with you a little bit later, but in just general terms can you tell us what you did during the mission with respect to each of the incidents that are set forth in the report? Just a very broad description of what you did?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: When I visited Mostar I visited each incident site and on the exact location I set up a tripod with a laser range finder, a military-grade laser range finder which is visible in one of the photographs in the report. And from that location I tried to identify which possibilities there would be for a sniper or a shooter to shoot from at the incident site. Taking into account the differences in new buildings or tree that is might have grown in the 10 years since the incident. Measuring up -- lasering the exact distance, which has a deviation of about two metres at 500 metres, so it can be two or -- two metres more or two metres less. And drawing up rough sketches of the situation itself, measuring up the angle towards the alleged shooting location with a compass. And that's -- that's about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have explained how you worked very well, but a crucial question is as follows: When you went to the sites were you familiar with the military situation in 1993, which is the time of the events? Were you familiar with the positions of units that were present in the field, namely the HVO, the ABiH, and the Serbs? Was this information integrated into your report, into your case study, or did you make these sketches, these plans, did you reach your conclusions without taking these various elements into consideration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wasn't familiar with the Mostar situation. I have been to Bosnia on two deployments, the first time with UNPROFOR to Simin Han [phoen], next to Tuzla, so I was more or less familiar with the overall situation. As so -- yeah, just the difference in warring factions, where the battlefield was. But not with Mostar in particular. I passed through Mostar on going into Simin Han and going back to the Netherlands just passing by in a truck. So I didn't get any glimpse of Mostar at that time. Not more than a glimpse of Mostar at the time. And the information I included on the equipment of the HVO is strictly from literature conclusions from photographs that were -- from newspapers and on the internet in which HVO, the HVO military was carrying those rifles in their hands on the photograph. But I wasn't familiar with the military situation at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you did not incorporate into your report the positions occupied by the HVO, the Serbs, and the BH Army, because obviously the point of departure of the shots is fundamental and the question is to know where they came from and who militarily occupied those positions. But you didn't deal with that aspect.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't deal with that aspect. From a military -- from my military background, I was able to identify all the shooting of -- the alleged shooting locations as being very dominating features within Mostar. So that they would be very suitable for military positions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Just to follow up more brutally, you did not worry about who could have shot from there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I just looked at it technically; was it possible and what type of rifle would have been used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Again, a follow-up question. Even if you had not worried about who could have shot from there, as Judge Trechsel just said, but you are able to indicate to determine from what kind of place the shot came.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, a lot of -- in most of the situations the layout of the structures around the location extremely limited the possibilities for the shooter to be at. So if we -- if we are going to go into depth in the report, I could explain why -- almost the only possibility to fire from would be the Stotina or Spanish Square or the glass house.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed, Mr. Mundis. You probably intended to go into the cases one by one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Well, I -- I am indeed intending on doing that, Your Honour. I am simply at this point, trying to follow the guidelines at least in part that were provided to us yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me ask one more question, sir, in terms of how the report was produced. Can you tell us how you actually produced the final version of your report based on the information that was provided to you and the information you obtained while you were in the field.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: After returning to the Netherlands I -- well, I tried to -- I tried to filter the information that I acquired in the field, and tried to -- you know, put up a form that incorporated the questions that the Tribunal wanted answered. So, you know, what would be -- just a short bit of text about the type of rifle, the type of ammunition, a part on the identification would have been possible to identify people at that distance. Just an overall layout of the situation, and from -- from my point of view, I added an appendix on the weapons that might have been used together with a short part on the ammunition that was used. A feature on the long-range shooting in general, the influences when you fire a shot at long range, and just a general introduction on sniping in general.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let's turn now to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Mundis, I have a technical question which I find important. I am not exactly familiar with English, Dutch or any other terminology, so I will describe what I mean. When you fix any of these weapons absolutely, and you shoot 100 shots, all in the same direction, what you get is not one big hole, but you get a dispersion or a diversion or variance; what would be the correct word, and how does that look in these cases? It depends, of course, on the distance. Could you give us more information about this, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The difference in -- the number of -- if it's a group of shots we just call it a group, just -- and the difference between the holes which the bullets may get just a target on a range, they're influenced from second to second wind conditions can change so that can alter the sight deviations. But also the most important one is the first shot that you shoot out of a rifle with a clean barrel, the barrel is still cold and we call that a cold-bore shot. Because the gases -- the gases that are produced within the bullet, the firing pin strikes the primer, the propellant starts to burn, and the heat -- the heat of the gases will push the bullet out of its casing and out of the barrel. In doing that, the period of time it gets out of its casing and barrel, the heat is also absorbed by the barrel, which means there will be less power because there is less heat to be taken up by the barrel. So that changes -- that means at longer ranges you get a difference in the height but there is a just a lot of factors that come into play when shooting at a long-range. Longer range.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Usually, at least that is what I have experienced, learned and experienced in shooting, no weapon is so perfect that at a distance of several hundred metres even perhaps not necessarily considering the wind, humidity in there and all that, the bullets will not all be in the same spot, and normally one produces pictures which show a dispersion which resembles a bit the curve of Gauss and then one -- there are is a terminology, and a standard to say at this distance so and so many shots are within this range, but in a larger and still a few are far off. Would you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct. It is caused by all -- by all these influences. Sniper rifles nowadays, and also sporting rifles, they have sort of a certificate of accuracy, so -- which they call minute of angle, which is at 100 metres 1.25 centimetres. So if a rifle is a half MOA, as we call it, accurate, it means that you can fire three or five shots within 1.25 centimetres. But it's not technically possible to at every time at a long distance get the bullets in the same hole. What we do is at a longer range we measure up the group and then determine the -- a difference --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: The mean distribution.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The mean distribution and use that as our information for next time we shoot at that distance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: And is it correct, Lieutenant, that the progression where the distance is geometric; that is to say, it augments by the square?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A question which is along the lines of the questions already posed. In theory, a sniper at a distance between four and 500 metres with his rifle and his optic sights, is he capable of hitting an individual at a certain point in his body, a specific point? For example, the heel of a leg, can he do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, from my personal experience it would be possible, but if he is hit at the heel, the sniper will probably just aimed at the person and the bullet ended up at the heel. So it's -- for -- in my unit we maintain for a head shot to have a certified head shot in case of a hostage situation. We don't give a guarantee above 300 metres so we would have to get closer to the target to hit the target at 300 metres. So it's very difficult to say, I'm going to hit him there, because -- because of all the conditions that come into play.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Does that mean then, because what you're saying is very important, does that mean then that at a distance above 300, 400 metres, it is impossible for a sharpshooter to pick a part of the body and hit it exactly? He would be actually targeting the body - is that what you said? - and then the bullet would hit either the head, the neck, the thorax, the leg. Or with a good weapon with a weapon that's already shot with the heat from the gases and by using optic sights, if one had all that and if one was targeting the head, he would hit the head; if he was targeting the arm, he would hit the arm; if he was targeting the leg, he would hit the leg. What can you tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That would be a very -- if you wanted to just wound the person, it would be very unwise at large -- of greater distances above 300 metres to aim at the person and say I want to shoot him in the arm. Because -- because of the spreading conditions, it's -- it -- the chances are too big that you might hit the body instead of the arm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Lieutenant van der Weijden, I'm going to turn now to weapons and ammunition, and this is covered -- this is covered in appendix A of your report, which if we want to put it up on e-court is page 43. This is P 09808. The report is P 09808, and page 43 in e-court. Sir, you have a copy of your report in front of you, do you not?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: If you could turn please to appendix A. Can you describe for us what appendix A sets forth, what information, what type of information is contained in this appendix to your report?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: In the -- in the appendix I tried to give an overall view of the -- of weapons that were used at the time. With their -- what their calibre was, what their maximum effective range was, which is different from their maximum range in total. It's just the effective range that -- that's when the shooter might have a reasonable chance of hitting the target. So the bullet will actually go a lot further, but with a very slight chance that you might hit the target and just with a general comment of what -- a general description of the weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, let me just ask you a follow-up questions, sir. First of all, what is the source of the information that's contained on this weapons chart that's appendix A to your report?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: The source is, as I have written on the last page, it's -- it's Jane's infantry weapons, which is a big book, which is describes basically all the infantry weapons of the world, which are currently in service along with their main characteristics and photos.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, line 2 of page 71 in capturing an answer to an earlier question, you say, "Weapons that were used at the time." And my question to you, sir, is, used by whom or used by which military forces?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: These were weapons used by the HVO. I realise that I didn't get any instructions as to who might have fired the shots, but I am aware of the case of course, that it's -- so I assumed for myself that the HVO was the point of interest. Most of the weapons were actually used by all warring factions but some weapons were specific for the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And again two follow-up questions: How do you know that these specific types of weapons were used by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: These two weapons I know of is they appeared in some literature, which is the book, "Stalk and Kill" by Adrian Gilbert in addition, as I have referred to earlier, from photographs at -- from that time, which show HVO soldiers with those weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You have also mentioned, Lieutenant, that most -- and again this is lines 22 and 23 of page 71, "Most of the weapons were actually used by all warring factions." Can you elaborate upon that part of your statement, and particularly in light of the comments box on the far right-hand side of appendix A?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Could you ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I note, sir, that in the comment part on the farther right-hand column of your report, some of these weapons are Soviet bloc or American made or western made. Can you elaborate upon that part of your report in light of what you told us that most of these weapons were used by all the warring factions?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Yugoslavia had a very active weapon industry, Asastafo [phoen], which was the main factory and the main supplier for the Yugoslav army, produced the M70 and the M76 and the M59. They were all present at the time the conflict started and were used by all factions as what's shown in news reports and photos in the media as well. For the western sniper rifles, from my experience and from military reports the Croatians -- this is somewhat on assumption on my side. The Serbs made up a lot of the -- of the medium and higher cadre of the Yugoslav army and therefore had more access to the former Yugoslavian army equipment. The Croats therefore had to procure more weapons from where they could be procured, such as the Steyr and the SIG-Sauer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, looking at the list of weapons, I have two observations to make. I can see that the M48 doesn't figure there. It's a weapon that the Defence brought up with several witnesses on several occasions. Do you know about this M48 rifle? What it is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The name -- I know -- I can't picture myself the exact weapon. I might recognise it when I see a picture of it, but, yeah, sometimes there can be differences.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence will certainly come back to the matter, but in looking at the photographs of the weapons, the first observation that I can make is that there are some weapons with tripods, which were probably used by snipers that are in a -- that are hidden. And then the SSG69, that's another weapon, and we have the impression that these are weapons that can be used by somebody who is standing, like Lee Oswald, Adelis [phoen], and so on, these people who had rifles like that and shot, and they were standing in a standing position. Now, are there different techniques for somebody who is crouching, shooters standing and shooters that are prone, in the prone position and in the standing position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first -- the photo -- the pictures of the rifles shown, is that page 71 or 72. Because in my report I don't have the -- the same numbers as.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: It's page 44 in e-court is appendix A, page 2.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So on page 44, the only weapon that would not be suitable for standing, shooting standing up, would be the M82 because it's too heavy, it's over 10 kilo, so that is a bit heavy for standing shooting up [sic]. But all rifles can be fired shooting -- for standing up. The only difference is the bi-pod aids the shooter in a prone position, so lying down. But if there is no -- for me personally, I prefer shooting from a sandbag instead of the bi-pod because with the bi-pod it is a different kick every time you fire. So the SSD69 is a very suitable sniper rifle but just doesn't have the bi-pod.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Again, Lieutenant van der Weijden let me ask you about the weapons that are contained on appendix A, the first page of that under the subcategory rifles. Which of these weapons listed under the rifles category would be suitable for a military sniper to use?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Well, that would be the difference between the Soviet approach or the former eastern bloc approach and the western approach. In the western approach, snipers have always -- snipers have always been equipped with a bolt-action rifle which is a more precise rifle in general, which allows the sniper to -- yeah, they usually have a longer range than semi-automatic rifles. The snipers in the western armies, as described in the introduction, are usually employed in a separate sniper platoon at the battalion level. The Soviets had a different approach, they had -- the Dragunov or the M76 which is similar in a lot of ways was mainly used at platoon level, so they placed their snipers at the platoon level, but the semi-automatic and therefore has less reach than a bolt-action rifle. Of course depending on the ammunition that is used.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Again, perhaps my question wasn't clear, but of the rifles listed, and there are eight rifles listed on appendix A, which of those are suitable for use in sniping?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: The ones that would be suitable would be the M76, the Steyr SSG69, the SIG-Sauer 2000 or 3000, the Dragunov could be suitable but is a bit of an overkill for shooting on people, and the H and K G3SG/1, those are all suitable. The ones that are not suitable for sniping are the M70 or the M59.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And why are the M70 and M59 not suitable for sniping in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: It's on two parts. As for semi-automatic, it can be used -- a semi-automatic sniper rifles they do exist and they do produce reasonable results. Depending on how you look at it, but it's the calibre mostly that makes the rifle not suitable for sniping. If I compare the round, the 7.62 times 39, the 39 stands for the length of the casing, and therefore also for the amount of propellant available for the bullet, if I compare that to the ammunition that is used in the Dragunov or the M76, which is the 70.62, which is the same calibre times 54, so it's the same calibre but with a longer case, the energy which the M76 has when leaving the barrel is more than 4.000 joule, and the energy the M70 has when leaving the barrel is 2.000 joule. So that's a big difference. At 500 yards the energy of the M70 would already have dropped 75 per cent to around 500 joule. At the same range, the M76 round would still have almost 2.000 joules, almost the same as the M70 had as zero -- when leaving the barrel. So that makes -- that's the big difference. And the M59 used the same ammunition as the M70, and the other concern is that the M70, although some versions do have a mounting platform for a night vision scope or a different type of scope, the basic sights of the weapon are open iron sights in -- which in my opinion are certainly not suitable for long-range shooting because they are comparable, the sights on those rifles are comparable to the sights found on the basic air gun. So it's a short sight line that's the distance between the dioptre or the open feed and the front post. So it makes it difficult to aim at a longer distance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And Lieutenant van der Weijden, of these rifles that you have identified as being suitable for sniping --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Petkovic. You will have ample time to ask questions later, but what was it you wanted to say?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just an explanation from the witness. The M76 rifle, would you read out the calibres it uses, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The calibres that the M76 uses, according to Jane's infantry weapons, so they were produced at some time is the 7.92 Mauser round, which is an older round from the Germans in World War II and older actually, a machine-gun produced in Yugoslavia. The 7.62 times 54 R, which is a Soviet round, and it was produced for export in 7.62 times 54 NATO, that's a NATO round, according to Jane's infantry weapons, of course.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One more question. You are here as an expert. Is it possible that a rifle uses 7.92 and 7.62 calibres? Look at the difference in calibre. Now, will this lower calibre just fall through the barrel, it will just fall through the barrel, the 7.62 one. Let me tell you this too: The 7.9 [as interpreted] millimetre is not used, so as an expert you could have seen that the two that are -- one rifle cannot use two different types of calibre. You can't put a big thing in a small hole, if I can put it that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I took note of that problem because in the Zastava 76 you say 7.92 Mauser, 7.62, 54 R, 7.62 51 millimetres, and there you say NATO. That was a question I asked myself too. The Zastava M76, can it use three types of ammunition of different calibres? And although the difference is slight between the 7.62 types, it is quite a lot with respect to the 7.92 Mauser, so that is the question I was asking myself too and wondering about.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't maybe make myself clear that much. The rifles were produced in those calibres, it doesn't mean that they were suitable for all calibres at the same time. So if you -- they made one rifle chambered because you would have a different chamber because it's a longer casing, so they wouldn't be able to fire all three rounds from one rifle. You would have three rifles basically the same, only the chamber difference for the 7.69, slightly bigger diameter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the Zastava M76 rifle had a chamber and a canon for the Mauser type, whereas another one could only use the 7.62, which means that the M76 could come in three different formats, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, Lieutenant van der Weijden, of these rifles that you have listed in appendix A and which you have indicated were suitable for sniping, which of those rifles to your knowledge, if any, were used by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: I believe at the time all rifles were present. But it would be very difficult to determine exactly which rifle was used at the time of -- for each incident, but it would be possible to determine what type of calibre was used. So it would be a group of rifles that could have been used for the incident, for the shot, instead of just specifying one rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: My question then, sir, is what the group of rifles that are among those listed on appendix A that you have identified as being suitable for sniping?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Those would be the rifles that I've read out before. It's the M76, the SSG 69, the SSG 2.000/3.000 - those are two models, actually - the Dragunov, and the G3 SG/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let's turn now to the next subsection of appendix A which lists two types of machine-guns. Can you tell us whether either of those two types of machine-guns would be suitable for sniping?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Well, the machine-guns, they can be used for sniping. It's -- it's not suitable, but from my experience with the machine-guns we have in the Dutch Army, it is possible, if you -- instead of using length ammunition, and you put one round on the feeding tray to hit a target at a longer range, so it is possible, but then again with the M70 it would be possible to at a long-range, hit a target, but you wouldn't have a guarantee, you would have a very small chance of hitting it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And the same question then, sir, with respect to the anti-aircraft canyon that you have listed at the very bottom of appendix A at the top of page 2 of that appendix. Would that be suitable for use in a sniping role?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: That would not be suited for a sniper role. It would be suitable for a ground role, so they are very -- very efficient, actually in a ground role, but they are not used in the sniping role.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can I ask you then, sir, why you included these two machine-gun types and this anti-aircraft canon in the report just for purposes of clarification?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: In case number 5, which -- let me just look for certain. Yeah, incident number 5, there was a case in which three females were shot within the apartment, so they were fired, shot at through the wall, and there was talk of explosions within the room. Therefore, you would have to use a larger calibre, which would be able to held some type of explosive or incendiary ammunition, which is -- produces or starts fire. And they only exist in the anti-aircraft or the larger machine-guns.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And again, Your Honours, Mr. President, for the record, incident 5 and incident 12 were removed from the schedule of sniping incidents based on the expert's report. So he has made reference to incident 5 as a result of this report incident 5 and incident 12 are no longer listed in the report but I believe his answer explains why those weapons are contained in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me just ask you perhaps one last very short line of questions before we take the next break. And that deals with ammunition, and what types of ammunition are suitable for use in sniping. And I know that this is contained on pages 4 and 5 of appendix A to your report. Can you just briefly tell us first of all, sir, what are the various subcomponents of a bullet?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Of a bullet itself, so it's not the round.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Actually, I misspoke. Let's talk about the round itself first.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Okay. The round itself consists of the bullet, the propellant, a shell which contains the propellant and a firing cap which contains the very sensitive explosive material which can cause the propellant starting to burn. The propellant doesn't explode, as is sometimes thought, but it burns. So it is made out of the components of the case or shell or casing and the bullet, and then the propellant within the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And again, for purposes of clarification, when you talk about the propellant, what would a layman consider the propellant to be, or how would a layperson refer to the propellant, generally?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Probably gunpowder, but gunpowder is older. New materials have been made. Gunpowder produced a lot of smoke at the time, but now they have, based on nitrocellulose, they have made gunpowder that is almost smoke free.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For those who aren't in the know, could you describe the exit of the projectile, the firing pin, the charge? Could you -- the primer? Could you describe what happens, in fact, before the projectile exits the barrel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When pulling the trigger a firing pin is released which strikes the firing cap within the firing cap there is a sort of -- the firing pin acts as the hammer and there is a little bent or a little metal surface which acts as an anvil, so very little explosive charge is within the firing cap, and between sort of the hammer and anvil, and that compression of the material starts, causes the material to cause a flash. That flash starts to burn, if -- the propellant starts to burn because of the flash. The flash, because of the gases that heat up, they want to expand, which pushes the bullet out of the -- out of the casing and out of the Chamber into the barrel. Within the barrel there is rifling, which is, for those people who have ever seen a James Bond movie, in the opening scene there is sort of a diaphragm, and that's what you would see if you look through a barrel. So it's a rifling that pushes the bullet and stabilises the bullet when it leaves the barrel. So that is the process in general of a rifle shot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And when the bullet exits the barrel, what speed does it travel at? How many metres per second?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It depends on the number of the -- the round, of course. For instance the 7.62 times 39, so the standard Kalashnikov round. I have it here. It depends, of course, on the -- which -- which factory produces it and what type of bullet it is but in general it leaves the barrel at about 700 metres a second, slightly above 700 metres, but the more suitable sniper rounds, they leave the barrel at over 800 metres. So 820, 860 metres per second, with zero velocity [sic].

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I have just a couple more questions about ammunition and then we could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At 860 metres per second, that a means that a target at about 400 metres can be reached in half a second. By a bullet travelling at that speed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That would be only possible in a vacuum, because of the wind resistance or the air resistance, which can be different because of humidity, the altitude at which the shot is fired causes the bullet to slow down. So at -- if there would be no gravity but just air resistance, at a great range you would be able to just pick the will you tell out of the sky because it had slowed down that much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: As seen from the target, first you would see the light, second the sound, or second the bullet and third the sound? Excuse me. Excuse me. In which order does the target get information of the shot? First it must be the light, and then the bullet and then the sound, or first the sound and then the bullet? I think it is above sound speed, but I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It depends on the type of ammunition. If you have subsonic ammunition that travels under the speed of sound, well, the bullet would be slower than the speed of sound. So it is -- depends on the range that the shooter is. But first typically it would be the flash, the muzzle flash or the smoke because you can see that at the speed of light, which is the fastest speed that we know, then there would be the bullet striking the target, and afterwards you would hear the -- the sound. But at closer ranges, so under 300 metres, the sound would almost -- of the shot would almost reach you simultaneously, with the bullet it would be just too -- too little time to clearly distinguish the two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. All of that information was very precise. Mr. Mundis, it is necessary to have our break.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we just correct some information? The speed of sound is 330 metres a second. If a bullet travels at 800 metres per second then it can cover 100 or 200 metres or 500 metres to its target. There will always be a difference between the point at which a bullet impacts. If the bullet hits the head the person will die, won't hear anything. If he is wounded then after a certain time he will hear the sound. If he is incapable of hearing the sound, whether it is a distance of 300, 400 or 500 metres, the speed of sound, which is twice the speed of sound [as interpreted], can never be simultaneous with the sound heard. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, do you agree with what the accused has just said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do agree to a certain point. As I explained, there will always be a difference in time between the bullet striking the target and the sound. But unfortunately our brain doesn't always cooperate. So for the senses to get the message through to the -- to the brain, and it's the same with -- with eyesight, for the brain it will -- for the person itself those will be at shorter distances, shorter ranges they could arrive in -- in the victim's perception at the same time. So it -- well, physically from a physics point of view, they would arrive at a different time, but for his perception it would be very difficult to distinguish the sound that -- yeah, can be the same thing for the victim.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: To put the issue very simply, by no way would the victim hear a sound and maybe even have a chance to put down his or her head before the bullet comes, that is completely illusory, right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Mundis, we have to have our break now. After the break we will have another hour at our disposal. Will one hour be sufficient for you to cover all the incidents for which we have sketches and various hypotheses concerns the weapons involved and the ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You had one other area to talk about and that was just some basic information about basic ballistics and trajectories and scopes and how to compensate for these matters, and then going through the various incidents. We will do the best we can with the time available, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We will resume at five past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have 55 minutes left. I'd to inform the parties that we have to stop at 7.00 p.m., and likewise tomorrow because we have worked overtime twice this week and that causes problems for the interpreters, other staff members. At 7.00 p.m. We have to stop. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, Lieutenant van der Weijden, can you very briefly describe -- you've told us the components of the round, can you tell us the bullet itself?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: The bullet itself, it's made up of a copper mantle, usually copper, there are some other, but mainly it's a copper coating around a lead core. And that's the usual, but if it's a full-metal jacket that's usually used in the army. Apart from that, within the army there is also a component bullet which still has a full copper coating, but inside there is a steel tip for better penetration. So it's made up out of two components within the core, a small steel tip, and just behind that the lead core of the bullet. The copper coating is primarily for anti-oxidation of the lead, but also for pushing the bullet into the grooves to get the right twist going through the barrel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, Lieutenant van der Weijden, I would like to ask you a few questions, a very few questions about basic ballistics and I would ask if perhaps the usher could hand the witness just some blank paper. We discussed yesterday or the day before sir using a big white board, but I think it might be easier if we put the paper there and everybody can observe that on their computer screens. Can you just draw a basic diagram of the trajectory that a bullet takes upon exiting the barrel of a rifle?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Well, if this would be just a barrel, just because it's physics and with the main influence of gravity, if a bullet goes out of a barrel it starts to go down and never goes above the barrel if the barrel is completely level. And because the problems that would cause at longer ranges because the bullet would be going into the ground, with the use of a scope or other sights, the bullet, the barrel is compensated for the range, so and with the sight above it, it would come together at a certain distance at which distance you know the line of sight, so the sight picture that the shooter would have would completely coincide with the bullet trajectory. This means, of course, that if you -- this -- incorrectly judge the distance, so if this would be 300 metres but the target would actually be at 250 metres, the bullet would strike above the target or higher in the target. If you would -- if the distance would be 350 metres, the line of sight, so that he thinks he would be aiming here, but the bullet would actually strike lower in the target. So it is very important to get -- to get the sight adjusted for the right distance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, can you please explain how the sight is adjusted to get to the right distance, as you put it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Yes, well, I will explain for an optical sight, just the basic shape of an optical sight as most people know it. It would be a tube like this, and if we would enlarge this within this circle, you would have a sort of a rubber O-ring, which holds a tube within the tube. So that's -- you know, this is the -- a glass lens, which -- it contains a glass lens. If you would look through it, it would contain the radical with which the shooter aims. On the scope itself there are controls or turrets. Those turrets are -- this one would be the elevation. It does hold a screw, if the screw -- the fret would be like this. If you would turn the turret like that, you would press this part, the tube, you would press it down, which would alter the line of sight compared to the -- the barrel. Is that adequate enough?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us what would physically happen to the sight as it's mounted on the rifle, if anything, as a result of making this adjustment on the screw of the sight?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Well, because the controls are done internally, I will go to the next page, so again just a basic set up of a scope, if the rifle is -- this would be the stock and just the rifle, it would mean that at the longer distance you would have to compensate by holding the barrel up. The side picture would go down, which would cause the shooter to get the right side picture, would cause the shooter to aim the barrel higher. So that would be the interaction between the sight and the barrel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us, sir --.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Perhaps I could ask those diagrams be given IC numbers, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Put your initials on the first one. And we will have an IC number for this first sketch.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will become IC 381.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And do the same for the second document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And a second number for this one.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The second sketch will become Exhibit IC 382.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Lieutenant van der Weijden, could you please tell us what factors will influence the bullet as it leaves the barrel of the rifle and travel the downrange?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: The main influence would be the gravity that pulls the bullet down to earth, which causes the bullet to drop. That would be the biggest influence. The part that I mentioned before, the air resistance, the thickness of the air causes more friction to the bullet, which slows the bullet more. So in a tropical country the bullet will slow down faster than in a temperate climate. In addition, the air at a higher altitude contains less molecules will slow down a bullet less than at sea level. The air at sea level is thicker, so more air resistance, so -- yeah, more slowing down of the bullet. And for the sideways correction, the big influence is the wind cross-examination. At 500 yards, which is approximately 450, 460 metres, for the 7.62 times 54 rounds, which is used in the -- in M76 or the Dragunov, at 500 yards, the deviation with a slight wind, which is just a small breeze, will already push the bullet out of its way 45 centimetres to the left or the right if the wind would be complete a cross wind. So a difference if it deviate, if the wind came from just -- just right behind you, in front of you, in coming from -- a 2.00 position, is that so that would push the bullet in a different way, of course so this is a cross wind, exact 90-degree angle. That is the big inference. There is another one shooting at an angle, upwards or downwards, which I can explain easily with a drawing. If the shooter would be up here, so this would be the rifle so the shooter would be up here and the target would be the circle at the bottom, he would measure the distance like this, but the gravity only pulls on the bullet for this distance. So either shooting up or down, you will -- it's the -- you will -- the bullet will always end up higher than you -- sorry. Than you intend. So yeah, it's just Pythagorus, or a simple calculation. You calculate the distance and set up the rifle for the distance, but it is actually only this distance that would be covered by the bullet ballistically.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Again, if you could sign that document and we would ask for an IC number for this sketch as well, please.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A number, please.
